t.3.71.1: Bṛhadaśva said: Then, in the evening, the people announced to King Bhīma that Ṛtuparṇa, of true valor, had arrived among the Vidarbhas.
t.3.71.2: At Bhīma's word, that king entered the city of Kuṇḍina, making all the ten directions, with the intermediate quarters, resound with the rumble of his chariot.
t.3.71.3: Then Nala's horses there heard that rumbling of the chariot, and hearing it they rejoiced, just as of old when they were in Nala's presence.
t.3.71.4: And Damayantī heard that rumbling of Nala's chariot, deep like the roar of a thundering cloud at the coming of the rains.
t.3.71.6: The peacocks perched on the palaces, the elephants standing in their stalls, and the horses too heard there the rumble of the king's chariot.
t.3.71.5: When Nala's horses were reined in by Nala as in former days, Bhaimī thought the rumble of the chariot was just like his, and so did the horses.
t.3.71.7: Hearing the rumble of the chariot, the elephants and the peacocks too cried out with upturned faces, O king, as if they had seen the rising of clouds.
t.3.71.8: As that rumble of the chariot, as if filling the earth, gladdens my heart, this must be Nala, the lord of the earth.
t.3.71.9: If today I do not see that Nala, whose face is like the moon, the hero of countless virtues, I shall without doubt perish.
t.3.71.10: If today I do not enter the embrace between the arms of that hero, so pleasant to the touch, I shall surely perish without a doubt.
t.3.71.11: If the Naiṣadha, whose voice is like the rumbling of thunderclouds and who shines like gold, does not come to me today, I shall perish without a doubt.
t.3.71.12: If that king of kings, who strides like a lion and can check a rutting elephant, does not come to me, I shall perish without a doubt.
t.3.71.13: I do not recall any untruth in the great-souled one, nor anything he left undone; nor any word of his that went stale, even in his casual moments.
t.3.71.14: My Naiṣadha is a lord, forbearing and heroic, gentle, restrained, the master of his senses; and in private he never stoops to anything base, as though he were a eunuch.
t.3.71.15: As I remember his virtues day and night, wholly devoted to him, this heart of mine, bereft of my beloved, is breaking with grief.
t.3.71.16: Lamenting thus, as though she had lost her senses, O Bhārata, she climbed up to the great mansion, longing to see Puṇyaśloka.
t.3.71.17: Then, in the middle courtyard, she saw King Ṛtuparṇa, lord of the earth, standing on his chariot together with Vārṣṇeya and Bāhuka.
t.3.71.18: Then Vārṣṇeya and Bāhuka, having descended from that excellent chariot, unyoked those horses and set the chariot in its place.
t.3.71.19: Having descended from the seat of his chariot, Ṛtuparṇa, the lord of men, approached Bhīma of terrible prowess, O great king.
t.3.71.20: Then Bhīma received him with the highest honor, though he had arrived suddenly and without apparent reason; Bhīma did not know of the scheme the woman had devised.
t.3.71.21: "What brings you here? Welcome to you," he was asked by the king, O Bhārata, for that lord of men did not know that he had come on account of his daughter.
t.3.71.22: And King Ṛtuparṇa, wise and of true valor, saw no king or prince there at all, nor any talk of a svayaṃvara, nor any gathering of brahmins.
t.3.71.23: Then the king, lord of Kosala, reckoning the matter in his mind, said to him, "I have come to pay my respects to you."
t.3.71.24: And King Bhīma, smiling, pondered in his mind the reason for his coming, for he had travelled more than a hundred yojanas.
t.3.71.25: Having passed by many villages, he did not learn how matters truly stood; the reason given for his coming was declared to be some trifling business.
t.3.71.26: Thinking, “This is not how it is,” the king honored him and dismissed him, saying again and again, “Please rest, you are weary.”
t.3.71.29: He unyoked those horses and tended them according to the rules of the science, and having soothed them himself, he sat down on the floor of the chariot.
t.3.71.28: When King Ṛtuparṇa had gone, O king, accompanied by Vārṣṇeya, Bāhuka mounted the chariot and went to the chariot-shed.
t.3.71.27: Honored and glad at heart, the king, pleased by his pleased host, entered the dwelling assigned to him, followed by the royal servants.
t.3.71.30: But Damayantī, stricken with grief, beheld the king Bhāṅgasvari, Vārṣṇeya the son of a sūta, and Bāhuka, so changed in form.
t.3.71.31: Vaidarbhī thought: "Whose is this rumble of a chariot? It was mighty, like Nala's, and yet I do not see the Naiṣadha."
t.3.71.32: Surely that very skill must have been learned by Vārṣṇeya; that is why the thunder of his chariot has become as mighty as Nala's.
t.3.71.33: Or is it that King Ṛtuparṇa too is just as Nala is, so that this rumble of his chariot is perceived as though it were the Naiṣadha's?
t.3.71.34: Having thus reflected, O lord of the people, Damayantī sent forth a female messenger in search of the Naiṣadha, O king.
